exam: A 28‑year‑old at 32 weeks presents with clear fluid loss for 20 h, no fever. What is your next step? — Give prophylactic antibiotics and give corticosteroids; monitor for infection.

How would you differentiate PROM from urinary incontinence in a low‑resource setting? — Perform sterile speculum exam for pooling, use nitrazine/ferning; urine dipstick will be positive for leukocytes.
Why is induction of labour recommended after 37 weeks of PROM? — Infection risk outweighs benefits of continued pregnancy; fetal lungs are mature.

A woman with PROM develops fever and uterine tenderness. Which antibiotic regimen is appropriate and why? — Ampicillin + erythromycin (or clindamycin) for broad coverage of GBS and anaerobes; safe in pregnancy.
What are the maternal and fetal complications of untreated PROM? — Maternal chorioamnionitis, sepsis; fetal distress, neonatal sepsis, preterm birth.
Explain why tocolysis is contraindicated in PROM with suspected infection. — Suppressing labour allows infection to ascend, increasing maternal and fetal morbidity.
In a setting without ferning test, how would you confirm PROM? — Rely on history, sterile speculum pooling, nitrazine test, and ultrasound for oligohydramnios.

What counseling would you give a woman with PROM at 38 weeks regarding delivery? — Explain that delivery is recommended to reduce infection risk; discuss induction options and signs to return urgently.
ai.title: Prolonged Rupture of Membranes
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM) is loss of amniotic fluid ≥18 h before delivery. It raises infection risk and may affect labour progress, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Higher risk with multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, genital tract infections
sections.p: Rupture of membranes (ROM) normally occurs at the start of labour. When it lasts 18 hours or more before birth, it is termed prolonged ROM. The main concern is ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) and fetal compromise.

b: Diagnosis: patient reports fluid loss + positive nitrazine or ferning test
Latency period: time from ROM to delivery; >24 h markedly raises infection risk
Gestational age dictates urgency: <34 weeks – aim to prolong; ≥37 weeks – deliver
sections.p: Diagnose PROM by history, sterile speculum exam and, if needed, bedside tests. Management balances infection prevention, timing of delivery, and fetal monitoring.

b: Common pathogens: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, anaerobes, HIV‑related opportunists
Complications: chorioamnionitis, neonatal sepsis, preterm birth, fetal distress
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, laboratory support may be limited, so clinical judgement and simple bedside tests are crucial. Prompt antibiotics and appropriate timing of delivery reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity.

t.b: Confirms source of fluid; positive pooling of clear fluid indicates ROM
Answers: is the fluid alkaline? Positive (blue) suggests amniotic fluid; false‑positives with blood or semen
Answers: does the fluid show characteristic fern‑like crystals? Positive confirms amniotic fluid; unavailable → rely on clinical signs
Answers: is the fetus tolerating the latency? Persistent tachycardia or decelerations suggest fetal compromise

b: Antibiotics: ampicillin + erythromycin (or clindamycin) for 48 h; chosen for broad coverage and safety in pregnancy; avoid aminoglycosides unless resistant organisms
Tocolysis only if <34 weeks and no infection; nifedipine preferred, avoid magnesium sulfate unless for neuroprotection
Corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity if <34 weeks and delivery expected within 7 days
Induction of labour at ≥37 weeks or earlier if maternal/fetal infection develops
If delivery not imminent and resources allow, hospitalise for observation; in low‑resource settings, use community health workers for daily temperature checks
sections.p: Treat infection, monitor mother and fetus, and decide timing of delivery based on gestational age and clinical status.

b: Urine: positive dipstick for leukocyte esterase, nitrites; no ferning
Vaginal discharge: usually non‑alkaline, no pooling on speculum
sections.p: Distinguish PROM from urinary incontinence, vaginal discharge, or premature rupture of membranes (ROM before 37 weeks).

b: False‑positive nitrazine → confirm with ferning or ultrasound for oligohydramnios
sections.p: Nitrazine can turn blue with blood or semen; ferning may be absent if fluid is scant. Rely on a combination of history, speculum findings, and repeat testing.

b: Prioritise maternal fever and fetal heart rate over gestational age when infection suspected
Explain why antibiotics are given even if labour is not yet indicated
